mainEntity.name: How long do porcelain veneers typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Porcelain veneers can remain in good condition for ten to fifteen years or longer in many cases, though this varies between individuals. Factors such as the quality of the original placement, how well the patient's bite was assessed, their oral hygiene routine, and habits such as teeth grinding all influence lifespan. There is no universally guaranteed duration, and any estimate provided during a consultation should be understood as a general guide based on clinical experience rather than a confirmed outcome. Regular monitoring by a dental professional helps identify any changes early.

mainEntity.name: Can composite veneers last as long as porcelain ones?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite resin veneers generally have a shorter lifespan than porcelain veneers, often requiring maintenance, polishing, or replacement within five to seven years. However, with diligent oral hygiene, careful dietary habits, and regular professional upkeep, composite veneers can perform well for a number of years. Their main advantages are that they are less expensive, can often be applied in a single visit, and require less tooth preparation. Whether composite or porcelain is more appropriate depends on clinical factors and individual patient goals, and this decision is best made following a professional assessment.

Porcelain veneers are highly resistant to staining on their surface due to the smooth, dense nature of the ceramic material. However, the adhesive resin at the margins of the veneer can absorb pigment from foods and drinks such as coffee, tea, and red wine. Composite veneers are more susceptible to surface staining throughout. Maintaining good oral hygiene, attending regular professional cleaning appointments, and moderating intake of strongly pigmented food and drink can help preserve the appearance of veneers. A dental hygienist can also polish veneers professionally to help restore and maintain their colour.

mainEntity.name: Do veneers affect the health of the underlying teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: When placed appropriately following thorough clinical assessment, veneers should not cause harm to the underlying teeth. The preparation process involves removing a small amount of enamel, which makes the process essentially irreversible. It is therefore important that veneers are not placed where underlying dental health issues remain unresolved. If gum disease, decay, or structural concerns are present, these should be treated first. Poorly bonded veneers can potentially allow bacteria to penetrate the margin, which is one reason why clinical precision and ongoing maintenance are so important for preserving the health of veneered teeth.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal for veneers to feel different after they are fitted?

acceptedAnswer.text: A degree of adjustment is common after veneer placement as patients become accustomed to the new contours of their teeth. Very minor bite adjustments may be made at a review appointment. Some temporary sensitivity can occur, particularly if enamel was prepared, as the tooth adjusts to the change. Persistent sensitivity, discomfort when biting, or a feeling that the bite is uneven beyond the initial settling period are worth raising with your dentist. These are not necessarily signs of a problem, but they should be evaluated professionally so that any minor adjustments can be made promptly.

mainEntity.name: Can veneers be repaired if they chip or crack?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, minor chips or cracks in composite veneers can be repaired chairside by adding new composite material and reshaping the surface. Porcelain veneers, being ceramic, are more difficult to repair once chipped — smaller repairs can sometimes be carried out using composite material to restore the shape, but a full replacement may ultimately be required if the damage is significant or the structural integrity of the veneer is compromised. The feasibility of repair depends on the location and extent of the damage, the material involved, and the condition of the bond. A professional assessment will clarify the most appropriate approach.
